items.good: The headings are the template's, in its order: the name, an opening under no heading (the idea in one sentence at 3-6, then the kind of thing - a command-line tool for macOS and Linux - whom it is for and the gain at 6-8), Example, Why organize-downloads, Requirements, Installation, Documentation, Development, License. Each section opens with its main point; each list item is one sentence, with its explanation after a blank line and indented under it (Requirements), and no item is in bold.

From the opening I can tell it is for me if my Downloads folder holds so many files I cannot find the one I want. It sorts the files directly in a folder into one folder per kind by extension, lists every move first without moving anything, never deletes, renames or overwrites, and can put back its last move on that folder; that idea is what sets it apart. The gain is finding the file in a folder of its kind, and the kind of thing is a command-line tool for macOS and Linux.

The example is a Downloads folder like mine, with a hidden file, a partial download, an unknown kind, a name already taken and folders already there. I see each run I type (no option, --move, --undo), the exact lines printed, and the tree before and after, ending with the folder as it was at first. I checked it holds together: the lines are in name order, budget.xlsx stays because Documents/budget.xlsx exists and so has no undo line, Images and Installers are made and then removed, and Documents stays.

Why sets the tool against three other ways - by hand (make each folder and drag each file), sorting by kind in Finder or Files (orders only the view, the files stay together), and rule-based organizers (you write the rules first) - and says what the tool does that each leaves to me. No benefit that every way gives comes first.

items.did: The Requirements were fine to follow: `python3 --version` printed Python 3.14.4 and curl was at /usr/bin/curl, and each requirement says how to check whether you already have it. The new macOS note on access to Downloads (181-183) fills the gap I raised last time. Then I ran the Installation's download address again: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lovaizu/playground/main/organize-downloads/organize-downloads` printed 404. `ls organize-downloads` shows only README.md and LICENSE, so there is still no tool.
items.lacking: The tool still cannot be installed: the download address on line 170 gives 404, `curl -fsSL` as written fails, and `chmod` then fails on a missing file. So I could not run `organize-downloads --help` or the Example's three runs, and could not check that they print what lines 33-39, 49-55 and 80-84 show. This cannot be fixed in the README alone: it needs the tool at that address, or the user's decision on the steering's open question about a build task.

items.did: I followed each link from organize-downloads/ again: `ls organize-downloads organize-downloads/docs` shows only README.md and LICENSE, and docs/ does not exist. LICENSE (README 197) is there: the MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 lovaizu, and the README names it as MIT.
items.lacking: docs/usage.md (fuller use), CHANGELOG.md (what changed in each version) and docs/architecture.md (the entrance for those who build it) are still not there, so the reader reaches none of the three. The places are named in the right sections and Development stands apart from Documentation, but the links lead nowhere. Also, LICENSE is still not committed on the branch (git status shows it untracked).

parts.good: Reads through once: what it does, the dry run, the safety promises and the undo, then whom it is for. Every word is plain.

Each run comes in the order I would type it, with its output in a block. Hidden files, partial downloads and the extension are each explained where they first appear. The note about folders already there (91-93) now comes after --move and --undo have both been shown, so it rests on nothing ahead. The command for another folder is in a block (98-100), and the kinds are in a table.
Each alternative is one item that says what it leaves to me. 'the table above' points back to a table I have already read.

Each requirement says why it is needed and how to check for it. Every command to run is now in its own block (133-135, 145-147, 153-155, 160-162). Line 157 says how ~/.local/bin looks once written out in full, so I can recognise it in $PATH.
The download commands, then --help, each in a block, then the first use told by pointing back to the Example I have read, and the macOS access prompt with what to do about it.
Two items, each naming what is in which page.
One sentence naming what the linked page holds.
Names the licence and where its text is.
The standard MIT text, with the copyright year and holder on line 3. It reads straight through.

items.good: Each part adds something new. The opening gives the idea and whom it is for; the Example shows the runs and output without saying the opening again; Why adds only the comparison with other ways; Requirements and Installation give only the setup steps, and point back to the Example for the first use instead of repeating it; fuller use is left to docs/usage.md. There is no reviewer-facing text, no history of decisions and no 'this README' talk.

items.did: I set the opening's promises (never deletes, renames or overwrites; lists every move without moving; puts back the last move on that folder) beside the Example, the table and the steering's AC1-AC12. I found no two statements that cannot both hold, and the wording gap I raised last time is closed: 'last move on that folder' (5-6) now matches 75. The facts about other tools hold as far as I can check them: macOS ships curl, on macOS python3 offers to install itself, and macOS asks a terminal for access to Downloads. I then tried to run the product, using the install as in B-4.
items.lacking: I could not check any statement about what the tool does against the tool: the download address still gives 404 and the work holds no tool, so the Example's output, the --help line and the moves stay untried.
